questions.stem: Which feature is found in prokaryotic cells but not in eukaryotic cells?
options: Ribosomes that carry out protein synthesis
A plasma membrane made of a phospholipid bilayer
A cell wall outside the plasma membrane
A nucleoid region holding a circular chromosome
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes have no nucleus; their single circular chromosome sits in a nucleoid region of the cytoplasm. Ribosomes and a phospholipid plasma membrane are found in every cell, and plant and fungal cells, which are eukaryotic, also have cell walls.

questions.stem: Which feature is used to classify a cell as eukaryotic?
options: It has ribosomes that make its proteins
It has a cell wall outside its plasma membrane
It stores its genetic information as DNA in chromosomes
Its DNA is enclosed in a membrane-bound nucleus
questions.explanation: Eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles; prokaryotic cells do not. All cells use DNA and ribosomes, and cell walls occur in bacteria as well as plants and fungi, so none of those features separates the two groups.

questions.stem: Which organelle is the site of the aerobic stages of cellular respiration, producing most of a cell's ATP?
options: Mitochondrion
Chloroplast
Ribosome
Golgi apparatus
questions.explanation: Mitochondria carry out the aerobic stages of cellular respiration, releasing most of the energy in glucose as ATP. Chloroplasts make glucose by photosynthesis rather than breaking it down, and plant cells contain mitochondria as well as chloroplasts.

questions.stem: In a chloroplast, what are the stacks of flattened membrane discs called?
options: Grana
Cristae
Stroma
Matrix
questions.explanation: Thylakoid discs are stacked into grana, which hold the chlorophyll that absorbs light. The stroma is the fluid around the grana. Cristae are the folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane and the matrix is the fluid inside a mitochondrion.

questions.stem: Which organelle receives proteins from the rough endoplasmic reticulum, then modifies and packages them into vesicles for export?
options: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
Nucleolus
Golgi apparatus
Lysosome
questions.explanation: Proteins made on the rough endoplasmic reticulum travel in vesicles to the Golgi apparatus, which modifies, sorts and packages them for secretion. The smooth endoplasmic reticulum makes lipids rather than processing proteins for export, and the nucleolus makes ribosomal RNA.

questions.stem: Which part of each phospholipid in the plasma membrane faces the watery cytosol or extracellular fluid?
options: The hydrophilic phosphate head
The hydrophobic fatty acid tails
The non-polar ends of the fatty acid tails
The hydrophilic fatty acid tails
questions.explanation: Phosphate heads are hydrophilic, so they face the water on both sides of the bilayer. The fatty acid tails are hydrophobic and point inward, away from water, which is why the bilayer blocks ions and polar molecules.

questions.stem: Which substance can diffuse directly through the phospholipid bilayer without the help of a membrane protein?
options: Oxygen
Sodium ions
Glucose
Amino acids
questions.explanation: Small non-polar molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide dissolve in the hydrophobic core of the bilayer and diffuse straight through. Ions such as sodium, and polar molecules such as glucose and amino acids, are repelled by the hydrophobic tails and need channel or carrier proteins.

questions.stem: What distinguishes active transport from facilitated diffusion?
options: It uses carrier proteins embedded in the plasma membrane
It moves only small non-polar molecules straight across the phospholipid bilayer
It moves substances down their concentration gradient
It moves substances against their concentration gradient using ATP
questions.explanation: Active transport uses energy from ATP to move a substance from low to high concentration. Both processes can use carrier proteins, so using a carrier is not what separates them. Facilitated diffusion moves substances down their concentration gradient without ATP.

questions.stem: Glucose enters a red blood cell through a carrier protein, moving from a higher to a lower concentration without any ATP being used. What is this process?
options: Osmosis
Simple diffusion
Facilitated diffusion
Active transport
questions.explanation: Movement down a concentration gradient through a membrane protein, with no ATP, is facilitated diffusion. It is not simple diffusion, because glucose is too large and polar to cross the bilayer itself. Active transport would need ATP, and osmosis is the movement of water.

questions.stem: A cube-shaped cell has sides of 2 µm. What is its surface area to volume ratio?
questions.explanation: Surface area is 6 × 2 × 2 = 24 µm² and volume is 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 µm³, so the ratio is 24:8, or 3:1. A 1 µm cube would give 6:1, and writing volume first gives the inverted 1:3.

questions.stem: Agar cubes with sides of 1 cm, 2 cm and 4 cm are left in dye. After ten minutes, dye has moved 0.2 cm in from every surface of each cube. Which conclusion is correct?
options: The 1 cm cube has the greatest proportion of its volume dyed
The 4 cm cube has the greatest proportion of its volume dyed
All three cubes have the same proportion of their volume dyed
The 2 cm cube has the greatest proportion of its volume dyed
questions.explanation: The undyed core of the 1 cm cube is 0.6 cm across, with a volume of 0.216 cm³, so about 78% of the cube is dyed; the 4 cm cube is only about 27% dyed. The largest cube does have the most surface area, but its volume is far greater still, so its surface area to volume ratio is the lowest. This models why small cells exchange materials more effectively.

questions.stem: Why is there a limit to how large a cell can grow?
options: As a cell grows, its plasma membrane thickens, so substances can no longer diffuse through it
As a cell grows, its volume increases faster than its surface area, so exchange cannot keep up
As a cell grows, its surface area increases faster than its volume, so it loses too much water
As a cell grows, its surface area to volume ratio rises, so substances enter too quickly
questions.explanation: Volume increases with the cube of a cell's length but surface area only with the square, so the surface area to volume ratio falls as the cell grows. A large cell's membrane cannot exchange materials fast enough for its volume. The ratio falls, rather than rises, with size.

questions.stem: How do membrane-bound organelles help a eukaryotic cell function despite being larger than a prokaryotic cell?
options: They let large polar molecules cross the outer plasma membrane without any transport proteins
They separate reactions into specialised compartments with their own membrane surfaces
They increase the outer surface area of the plasma membrane around the cell
They reduce the total volume of the cell, so its surface area to volume ratio rises
questions.explanation: Organelles divide a large cell into compartments, each with the enzymes and conditions for particular reactions, and their internal membranes add surface for those reactions. They are inside the cell, so they do not add to the outer membrane or reduce the cell's volume.

questions.stem: A cell has a cell wall, ribosomes, a nucleus, mitochondria and a large central vacuole, but no chloroplasts. Which cell could it be?
options: A human white blood cell
A palisade mesophyll cell of a leaf
A cell from the root of a plant
A bacterial cell from the soil
questions.explanation: A cell wall and a large central vacuole point to a plant cell, and root cells receive no light so they lack chloroplasts. A palisade mesophyll cell is packed with chloroplasts. A bacterium has no nucleus or mitochondria, and animal cells have no cell wall.

questions.stem: Pancreatic cells that secrete large amounts of digestive enzymes would be expected to contain plenty of which organelles?
options: Chloroplasts and a large central vacuole
A nucleoid region and plenty of free ribosomes for protein export
Rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum and lysosomes
questions.explanation: Digestive enzymes are proteins made for export, so these cells need ribosome-studded rough endoplasmic reticulum to make them and Golgi apparatus to package them for secretion. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum makes lipids, not proteins, and chloroplasts and nucleoids are not found in animal cells.

questions.stem: A red blood cell is placed in distilled water. What happens to it?
options: Water enters by osmosis, and the cell swells and may burst
Water leaves by osmosis, and the cell shrinks and crenates
Salts leave by osmosis until the concentrations are equal
Its cell wall stops the cell from changing in volume
questions.explanation: Distilled water is hypotonic to the cell, so water moves in by osmosis toward the higher solute concentration inside. With no cell wall to resist it, the red blood cell swells and can burst. Osmosis is the movement of water, not of salts.

questions.stem: A plant epidermal cell is placed in a concentrated salt solution. What would be seen under a microscope?
options: The cell swells until the cell wall bursts open
The central vacuole enlarges as water is drawn in
Salt enters the cell and the cell becomes more turgid
The cytoplasm and plasma membrane pull away from the cell wall
questions.explanation: The salt solution is hypertonic, so water leaves the cell by osmosis and the vacuole shrinks. The plasma membrane pulls away from the rigid wall, which is plasmolysis. Swelling and turgor happen in a hypotonic solution, not a hypertonic one.

questions.stem: Uptake of substance X by a cell rises as its outside concentration increases, then levels off at high concentrations. A drug that stops ATP production has no effect on uptake. How does X most likely enter?
options: By facilitated diffusion through carrier proteins
By active transport through protein pumps
By simple diffusion through the phospholipid bilayer
By osmosis through aquaporin channels
questions.explanation: Levelling off shows the carrier proteins are saturated, and the lack of effect of the drug shows no ATP is needed, which together indicate facilitated diffusion. Active transport would slow when ATP production stopped. Simple diffusion would keep rising with concentration rather than levelling off.

questions.stem: Root hair cells hold a higher concentration of nitrate ions than the soil water, yet keep absorbing nitrate. When oxygen is removed from the soil, nitrate uptake falls sharply. What best explains this?
options: Nitrate enters by facilitated diffusion, which needs oxygen to open channels
Nitrate enters by osmosis, which stops when the soil water lacks oxygen
Nitrate enters by simple diffusion, which slows as the oxygen leaves
Nitrate enters by active transport, which needs ATP from aerobic respiration
questions.explanation: Nitrate is moving against its concentration gradient, which requires active transport, and the ATP for it comes mainly from aerobic respiration. Without oxygen, ATP supply drops and so does uptake. Facilitated diffusion only moves substances down a gradient, so it could not explain uptake here at all.

questions.stem: Cells lining the kidney's collecting ducts move large volumes of water quickly across their membranes. Which membrane component makes this possible?
options: Cholesterol molecules spread through the bilayer
Sodium–potassium pumps that use ATP
Glycoproteins on the outer membrane surface
Aquaporins, which are channel proteins for water
questions.explanation: Water can cross the bilayer slowly by itself, but aquaporins are channels that let it move by osmosis far faster. Sodium–potassium pumps move ions, not water, and glycoproteins act in cell recognition.

questions.stem: Which statement describes binary fission in bacteria?
options: Homologous chromosomes pair up and separate to form four cells
A small outgrowth containing a copy of the DNA buds off the cell and later detaches
The circular chromosome is copied, and the cell divides into two identical cells
A spindle separates the sister chromatids into two new nuclei
questions.explanation: In binary fission the circular chromosome is replicated, the copies move apart as the cell lengthens, and the cell splits in two. There is no nucleus or spindle, which are features of mitosis in eukaryotes. Pairing of homologous chromosomes happens in meiosis.

questions.stem: Why can a population of bacteria grow faster than a population of dividing eukaryotic cells?
options: Binary fission has no nucleus to divide or spindle to build, so each division is quicker
Binary fission produces four daughter cells each time rather than two
Bacteria skip copying their DNA before they divide by binary fission
Bacteria divide by mitosis, which takes less time than binary fission because there is no S phase
questions.explanation: Binary fission is simpler than the eukaryotic cell cycle: one circular chromosome is copied and the cell splits, with no nuclear envelope to break down or spindle to form. It still produces two cells, and the DNA must still be copied first so each daughter cell gets a full set.

questions.stem: During which stage of the eukaryotic cell cycle is DNA replicated?
options: S phase of interphase
G1 phase of interphase
G2 phase of interphase
Prophase of mitosis
questions.explanation: DNA is synthesised in S phase, so each chromosome then consists of two identical sister chromatids. In G1 the cell grows and makes proteins, and in G2 it prepares for division. By prophase the DNA has already been copied and is condensing.

questions.stem: During which phase of mitosis do sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles of the cell?
options: Metaphase
Prophase
Telophase
Anaphase
questions.explanation: In anaphase the centromeres split and spindle fibres pull the sister chromatids to opposite poles. In metaphase they are still joined and lined up at the equator, and in telophase new nuclear envelopes form around the two sets.

questions.stem: A dividing cell shows condensed chromosomes lined up along its equator, each attached to spindle fibres at its centromere. Which phase is this?
options: Prophase
Telophase
Metaphase
Anaphase
questions.explanation: Chromosomes aligned at the equator with spindle fibres attached at the centromeres is metaphase. In prophase the chromosomes condense and the nuclear envelope breaks down, but they have not yet lined up. In anaphase the chromatids have already started to separate.

questions.stem: Which event happens in prophase of mitosis?
options: Chromosomes condense and the nuclear envelope breaks down
New nuclear envelopes form around two sets of chromosomes
Sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles of the cell
The cytoplasm divides to form two separate cells
questions.explanation: Prophase begins mitosis: chromosomes coil up and become visible, the nuclear envelope breaks down and the spindle starts to form. Nuclear envelopes reform in telophase, chromatids separate in anaphase, and cytoplasm divides in cytokinesis.

questions.stem: How does cytokinesis in a plant cell differ from cytokinesis in an animal cell?
options: A cell plate forms from vesicles at the equator, instead of a cleavage furrow
A cleavage furrow pinches the cell in two, instead of a cell plate forming
The cytoplasm divides before mitosis begins, instead of after it
The nucleus divides during cytokinesis, instead of during mitosis
questions.explanation: A rigid cell wall stops a plant cell from pinching in, so vesicles from the Golgi apparatus gather at the equator and fuse into a cell plate that becomes the new wall. Animal cells divide by a cleavage furrow, a ring of protein filaments that pinches the cell in two.

questions.stem: A human body cell in G1 has 46 chromosomes. How many chromatids does it have at metaphase of mitosis, and how many chromosomes will each daughter cell have?
options: 46 chromatids; 23 chromosomes
92 chromatids; 23 chromosomes
46 chromatids; 46 chromosomes
92 chromatids; 46 chromosomes
questions.explanation: After S phase each of the 46 chromosomes has two sister chromatids, giving 92 at metaphase. When the chromatids separate, each daughter cell receives 46 chromosomes, the same number as the parent cell. Halving to 23 happens in meiosis, not mitosis.

questions.stem: In 200 onion root tip cells, 160 were in interphase, 20 in prophase, 6 in metaphase, 8 in anaphase and 6 in telophase. If the cell cycle takes 20 hours, about how long does prophase last?
options: 2 hours
4 hours
16 hours
1 hour
questions.explanation: The share of cells in a phase reflects the share of time spent in it: 20 of 200 cells is 10%, and 10% of 20 hours is 2 hours. Dividing 20 hours equally among five stages gives 4 hours, which ignores the data. 16 hours is the length of interphase.

questions.stem: What is checked at the G1 checkpoint of the cell cycle?
options: Even sharing of organelles, before the cytoplasm divides
Cell size, nutrient supply and DNA damage, before DNA is replicated
Attachment of every chromosome to spindle fibres, before anaphase
Completion of DNA replication, before the cell enters mitosis
questions.explanation: The G1 checkpoint decides whether the cell is ready to commit to copying its DNA. Checking that DNA replication is complete happens at the G2 checkpoint, and spindle attachment is checked at the metaphase checkpoint during mitosis.

questions.stem: A mature nerve cell no longer divides. In which phase of the cell cycle does it remain?
options: S phase
Prophase
G0
G2
questions.explanation: Cells that leave the cycle and stop dividing enter G0, a resting phase in which they still carry out their normal functions. G2 and S phase are part of active preparation for division, and prophase is part of mitosis itself.

questions.stem: What is apoptosis?
options: Uncontrolled cell death caused by injury
Division of the cytoplasm after mitosis
Uncontrolled division of cells with damaged DNA
A regulated, programmed process of cell death
questions.explanation: Apoptosis is programmed cell death, a controlled sequence that removes unwanted or damaged cells, for example the webbing between developing fingers. Uncontrolled death from injury is necrosis, and uncontrolled division is a feature of cancer.

questions.stem: Which observation shows a cell is dying by apoptosis rather than by necrosis?
options: The cell takes in water by osmosis until its plasma membrane ruptures
The cell's lysosomes burst and its contents leak into the surrounding tissue
The cell shrinks and breaks into membrane-bound fragments that phagocytes engulf
The cell swells and bursts, releasing its contents and causing inflammation
questions.explanation: In apoptosis the cell shrinks, its membrane blebs and it breaks into apoptotic bodies that phagocytes remove, so no contents spill and there is no inflammation. Swelling, bursting and leakage of contents are signs of necrosis.

questions.stem: What starts the extrinsic pathway of apoptosis?
options: The release of cytochrome c from the cell's damaged mitochondria
Detection by the cell itself of damage to its own DNA
Rupture of the cell's own lysosomes, which releases digestive enzymes into the cytosol
A signal molecule binding to a death receptor on the cell surface
questions.explanation: The extrinsic pathway is triggered from outside the cell when a signal molecule, often from an immune cell, binds a death receptor in the plasma membrane. Internal damage and the release of cytochrome c from mitochondria belong to the intrinsic pathway. Both pathways then activate caspases.

questions.stem: A drug blocks every caspase in a cell that has just received a signal to undergo apoptosis. What is the most likely result?
options: Apoptosis still happens, because the death receptor dismantles the cell
Apoptosis cannot proceed, because caspases dismantle the cell
Apoptosis is quicker, because caspases normally hold it back
The death receptors are lost, because they are made of caspases
questions.explanation: Caspases are protease enzymes that carry out apoptosis by breaking down the cell's proteins from within. Without them the signal cannot be carried through to the breakdown of the cell. Caspases are activated inside the cell after the receptor is bound; they are not the receptors themselves.

questions.stem: Which is a characteristic of cancer cells?
options: They keep dividing without growth signals and avoid apoptosis
They stop dividing as soon as they touch neighbouring cells
They become more specialised than the cells around them
They divide only after receiving a growth factor signal
questions.explanation: Cancer cells divide uncontrollably, ignore stop signals and escape apoptosis. Normal cells stop dividing when they contact their neighbours, but cancer cells lose this contact inhibition and pile up. Cancer cells usually become less specialised, not more.

questions.stem: What is the usual effect of a mutation that turns a proto-oncogene into an oncogene?
options: The cell cycle halts permanently at the G1 checkpoint
The cell undergoes apoptosis earlier than it should
The cell stops replicating its DNA in S phase before it divides
Cell division is stimulated even without growth signals
questions.explanation: Proto-oncogenes code for proteins that promote cell division. An oncogene is an overactive form that keeps signalling the cell to divide, like an accelerator stuck down. Halting the cycle and triggering apoptosis are jobs of tumour suppressor genes.

questions.stem: The p53 protein halts the cell cycle when DNA is damaged and can trigger apoptosis if repair fails. What is a mutation that inactivates both copies of the p53 gene most likely to do?
options: Make cells undergo apoptosis even when their DNA is undamaged
Stop all cell division, so damaged tissues can no longer be renewed
Make p53 an oncogene that produces extra growth factor signals
Let cells with damaged DNA keep dividing, raising the risk of cancer
questions.explanation: p53 is a tumour suppressor: it acts as a brake on the cell cycle. With no working p53, damaged cells are neither held at the checkpoint nor removed by apoptosis, so mutations build up. Losing the brake does not cause extra apoptosis or stop division; it allows unchecked division.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a malignant tumour from a benign tumour?
options: Its cells all die by apoptosis once the tumour is large
Its cells can invade nearby tissue and spread to other sites
Its cells divide by mitosis rather than by binary fission
It stays enclosed in a capsule at its original site
questions.explanation: Malignant tumours invade surrounding tissue and can metastasise, spreading through blood or lymph to form new tumours. A benign tumour stays in one place, often within a capsule. Cells of both kinds divide by mitosis.

questions.stem: Which two properties define a stem cell?
options: Full specialisation and the ability to divide
Totipotency and the ability to form a placenta and embryo
Self-renewal by division and the ability to differentiate
Rapid division and resistance to apoptosis
questions.explanation: A stem cell is unspecialised, can divide to renew itself, and can differentiate into specialised cell types. Many stem cells, such as those in bone marrow, are not totipotent, so totipotency is not part of the definition. Resistance to apoptosis is a feature of cancer cells.

questions.stem: Which cells are totipotent?
options: The zygote and the cells of its first few divisions
The cells of the inner cell mass of a blastocyst
The stem cells found in adult bone marrow
The induced stem cells made from skin cells
questions.explanation: Totipotent cells can form every cell type, including the placenta and other extra-embryonic tissues; only the zygote and its earliest descendants can do this. Inner cell mass cells, and stem cells induced from skin cells, are pluripotent: they can form all body cells but not the placenta.

questions.stem: Cells from the inner cell mass of a five-day-old human blastocyst are grown in culture. Which outcome is possible?
options: They form only blood cells, like bone marrow stem cells
They form only more cells of the inner cell mass
They form nerve, muscle and blood cells, but not placenta
They form every cell type, including the placenta
questions.explanation: Inner cell mass cells are pluripotent: they can become any cell of the body, but by this stage the outer layer of the blastocyst has taken on forming the placenta. Forming the placenta as well would require totipotency, which only the zygote and its earliest cells have.

questions.stem: Stem cells in bone marrow are multipotent. What does this mean?
options: They form only one cell type, as well as renewing themselves
They form several related cell types, such as all the blood cells
They form every cell type of the body except the placenta
They form every cell type of the body, including the placenta
questions.explanation: Multipotent stem cells are limited to a family of related cell types; blood stem cells form red cells, white cells and platelets. Forming every body cell except the placenta describes pluripotency, and adding the placenta describes totipotency.

questions.stem: A muscle cell and a nerve cell from the same person contain the same genes, yet differ in structure and function. Why?
options: Different genes are switched on and expressed in each cell type
Each cell type lost the genes it does not use during mitosis
Mutations during development gave each cell type different genes
Each cell inherited a different half of the person's chromosomes
questions.explanation: Differentiation happens through gene expression: each specialised cell switches on the genes it needs and silences others. Mitosis gives every body cell a complete, identical set of genes, so nothing is lost and the cells do not receive different halves.
